::: {.callout-note}
The designs on this page are historical. They are included so future agents
can see what was already considered and why a new study would need a distinct
question or evidence source.
:::

# July coupled-regression designs

The 13 July designs specified a joint pressure/speciation objective, frozen
parameter bounds, grouped data partitions, multistart behavior and explicit
identification checks. The independent-assessment design separated fitting
rows from comparison rows and required coverage and failure accounting.

These documents recorded the estimation strategy and acceptance questions at
that stage. Later studies changed the active coordinates, model choices and
assessment sequence. The designs were never a parameter adoption and should
not be rerun simply because their prose is older.

# What was learned afterward

The 28 July shared-ion density/speciation fit produced a stable converged
solution but worsened pressure. In its exact retained metric, pressure
training/active median absolute log error changed **0.432 → 0.869** and the
reserved comparison changed **0.542 → 0.730**. The August pressure-first
screening explored directions, conditioning, bounds and loading trends without
resolving the coupled fit. The consolidated Issue 70 comparison therefore
recorded a supported-negative decision rather than exporting transferable
parameters.

The later reaction-temperature study changed the question: EOS parameters were
held fixed while two sensitivity directions spanning pressure, speciation and
heat were tested. It improved pressure and heat more than speciation and left
carbamate/bicarbonate partition unresolved. That is the current retained
lesson from the sequence.

# How to use this history

Use the July records to avoid repeating objective-design work. A new numerical
study needs to state what changed in the question, inputs, model/Engine
identity or evidence. It must retain the exact data partition, evaluated and
failed states, residual definitions, parameter identity and independent
assessment rule. A historical design is retained background; it is not permission to
revive a discarded strategy or to promote its vector.
